title: What you should learn before trying to ship an AI game.
author: Embarrassed_Text_347
selftext:
Hello all,

What do you think is the most critical thing people need to learn before building/shipping AI games? This is an open discussion, I'm curious to hear other's thoughts as well on this topic. 

I wanted to make a post to help out others who are just starting out. 

AI is a great tool, when used with proper management. From what I see on a majority of projects, the ui and ux are some of the biggest issues when it comes to generative AI games. I urge any of you who do not have practical experience building out ui/ux to spend just a few hours watching a few youtube videos/courses on it. It will improve your games/websites DRAMATICALLY. One of the biggest immediate indicators of separating the ai slop from a professional is ui/ux. Does the menu layout make sense? Does the color scheme match the type of game you're creating or vibe you're trying to give off? Are there hover effects, haptics, keyboard shortcuts, accessibility settings, etc. 

Not every project should have massive bright rainbow-themed buttons. Pick a theme and stick to it, you don't need to incorporate every color in existence into your game's design. You should really hone in on 2-3 core colors max. You can still have variation, but vary one of those core colors, rather than just picking a new one. For example, use a normal, light, or dark version of the core color.

Many of these things can be fixed very easily, and it makes the game feel so much better and won't give off slop vibes. 

For others, what else do you think beginners/intermediates need to focus on to level up their creations?

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body:
I've mentioned in other posts, but you have to know the limits of the tools and skills you have at your disposal. Given my tiny budget and tight timeline, AI tools are the only real option. Given that, the game needs believable constraints to reduce performance demand, making up for the lack of animations, and a reason you can't get TOO close to surfaces.

Now that I'm in the end stages, I'm very glad I had these foresights, as every one came true.

replies.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
replies.body: I believe the limit of the tools is highly dependent on the person using them. Someone who has a lot of exp in web dev, game dev, etc. using only ai will still make an incredibly better project than someone with little to no exp using the same tools.

comments.author: joeld42
comments.body: Don't do a big project, start with something incredibly small and scoped and finish it. This is a lot easier than it used to be with AI but there's still a million rabbit holes you can get lost down, and AI makes scope creep more likely than ever.

comments.author: doudou262
comments.body:
100% on UI/UX - it's the instant slop detector. You can have genius AI under the hood but if it looks like a 2008 PowerPoint with 7 neon buttons fighting each other, nobody's sticking around.

My add: AI is an incredible builder but a terrible game designer. It'll happily give you 10 mediocre features instead of 1 addictive loop, so nail the feel first - juice, timing, one core loop that actually slaps - then let AI help you scale the polish.

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
Learn game design. Really learn it. Mechanics, difficulty curves, achievements everything.

Same with gen-AI art. If you don't understand art, you will make slop. If you understand, you can prompt better and notably judge better.

comments.author: Vindelator
comments.body:
If you built a game in a day, don't brag.

I understand the temptation.

It's one thing to demo some tech or workflow, but take your time.

A rushed game is a slop game.

comments.author: ericoinen
comments.body:
Agreeing on UI, and adding the one thing that is invisible in a screenshot and obvious after ten minutes of play: decide, before you build anything, which facts the model is allowed to own.

In a generative game what reads as slop is usually not the prose and not the buttons, it is the world contradicting itself. Health that was 4 and is now 9 with no explanation. An NPC who forgot he is dead. An item used twice. Players forgive dull writing far faster than they forgive a world that does not remember.

The practical form: the model describes, the code decides. Numbers, inventory, positions, time, who is alive, all of it lives in ordinary state that ordinary code mutates, and the model reaches it only by calling a function that either succeeds or is refused. When a player tries something the state does not allow, that refusal is the interesting part of the game. If the model is the one holding the numbers, it will just agree with the player instead, every time.

Two things fall out of this and both are worth having early:

* Show the state changes. One visible line per change costs almost nothing, and it is the fastest way for a player to learn the world is real, and for you to find the bug when it is not.
* Your tests become possible. You cannot regression test prose, but you can absolutely test that a failed check never raises a stat.

Cheapest way to find out whether your project has this problem: play your own game for twenty minutes, write down every number you see on screen, then check them against your logs. Everything that disagrees is what a reviewer will call slop without being able to say why.

comments.author: Arcayon
comments.body: Learn how to use Plan Mode. Hopefully a simple concept for those experienced with agentic, but I bet more than half of you are still copying and pasting code.

comments.author: Gigaslavx
comments.body: I say not being delusional that you will succeed on a cheapskate 20 dollar plan when everyone including their grandmothers are shipping ai slop in masses even if your game somehow unlikely ends up good you need a ton on marketing most lack most skills if you good you good

comments.author: TaylorCooper337
comments.body: Try to setup your project yourself and get as far as you can. Understand your architecture and use real assets. Then if you can't figure something out, go for it in small steps. I don't think people should "Vibe Code" games and the whole "Look at this one prompt game" stuff is braindead imo.
